source.title: Re-examining learning linear functions in context
source.authors: Omar Naim; Guilhem Fouilhé; Nicholas Asher

record.tranche_reason: The study varies training and test distributions and measures in-context linear-function prediction performance, a different way of testing the data-dependence part of V5. It does not identify or intervene on induction heads.
record.gate_note: The study reports ICL performance under distribution shifts, which bears on V5's claim about whether ICL persists across training setups. Its attention-weight analysis and comparison with a nearest-neighbor proposal do not identify or test induction heads, and it does not measure loss by token index or few-shot task learning. Results cited from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study never identifies, measures or ablates induction heads or previous-token heads. It does not track formation over training or measure loss by token index. Its results are linear-function ICL error under train/test distribution shift in small transformers trained from scratch. That is out-of-distribution generalization of a trained ICL ability, not whether induction heads form or whether ICL persists or emerges as a function of training data (V5). Its only link to the original source is an argument that a 3-nearest-neighbour averaging rule it attributes to Olsson et al. does not match model outputs (Sec. 6, App. G). That concerns a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude their models achieve in-distribution ICL (ICL1) but not robust inference of the linear class (ICL2), so they do not implement linear regression. Predictions are capped by training-determined boundary values, giving an accuracy–generalization trade-off. Attention layers are necessary and sometimes sufficient. They also reject a nearest-neighbour averaging account attributed to Olsson et al. and propose their own projection hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains small transformers from scratch on synthetic linear-function prediction and evaluates distribution shifts. It does not use induction-head detection, mechanistic circuit analysis, or training-time induction-head measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance changes with training and test distributions, prompt ordering, and model size; sorted prompts improve some out-of-distribution results.

fits_no_version.finding: Small softmax transformers learn in-distribution linear-function ICL, but error rises non-linearly as the test function distribution widens. Predictions saturate at training-determined boundary values; wider training improves range but lowers small-value accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ICL of linear functions in small transformers is bounded by training-range boundary values rather than implementing linear regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Model predictions differ substantially from a 3-nearest-neighbour averaging rule the authors attribute to Olsson et al. (3NN rows in Tables 1–2; App. G examples). This is used to argue that rule does not describe the task's mechanism. Note the 3NN row as tabled is the averaging method's own error, not model behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A nearest-neighbour copying/averaging account of ICL does not explain linear-function regression ICL.

record.problems: The models are small synthetic-task transformers, so the results do not establish behaviour in large language models. The study does not measure induction heads, and reports no uncertainty estimates for the listed error results.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional model-by-test-distribution results in Tables 1–5 and additional figures, including other architectures, training distributions, sorted prompts, and attention-only models. The selected rows record the 12L8AHN test-distribution sweep, the authors' all-model statement, and the explicitly stated training-variance trade-off; the remaining detailed model-specific table entries are omitted.

untested.parts: All: no induction or previous-token heads identified, no composition analysis, no [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying.
All: no training-time onset, abruptness, loss bump or co-timing analysis.
All: no induction heads, no large models, no loss-by-token-index measure.
All: induction behaviour not measured in any model.
Whether and when induction heads form and whether ICL persists as a function of training data. Only OOD test error after training is measured.
All: no head-level attribution of few-shot task learning.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 link conflates test-time distribution-shift robustness with V5's data-dependence of induction-head formation and ICL persistence. No row bears on any version. Baselines in R1–R10 were copied from the Table 2 y=0 reference (Dit=N(0,1)), while the values come from Table 3, whose caption states Dit=U(-1,1) with y=0 reference 1.52…128.52.

versions.untested_parts: Induction-head formation, composition with a previous-token head, and [A][B] … [A] → [B] copying.
Training-time onset, abruptness, loss-curve bump, and timing relative to in-context-learning gains.
Induction heads as the mechanism for most in-context learning in large transformers, including loss falling with token index.
Induction behaviour across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Whether and when induction heads form. The study tests how training and evaluation distributions affect linear-function ICL performance, not whether induction heads form or persist.
Whether few-shot task learning is carried mainly by mechanisms other than induction heads.
Whether induction-head formation comprises multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.
